heading: Java waits for a real Yon endpoint
summary: A Java HTTPClient is an interface whose methods have no body, such as `Greeting read();`. Tachyon writes the method and reads the answer into the record `Greeting` from `client/models`; an answer of another shape gives a `Behaviors.Failure` whose code is `HTTP_RESPONSE`, and a failed request gives the code of the browser transport, such as `HTTP_STATUS`. A service gets the client from a `private final GreetingClient greetingClient;` field with `@Needs` on the line above, and calls it from an ordinary method. Java has no async keyword: Tachyon runs each call of a service method in its own TeaVM fiber. When the method does not wait, the page gets its answer at once. When it waits for the server, the page keeps working, other calls to the service run, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. A getter, a setter or `OnStart` cannot wait: a request there fails with `HTTP_REQUEST`. `GreetingSetup` adds no adapter, so the request goes to the server of the page: the same origin, without cookies. `Cached` lets the browser cache answer a read, and after a successful `ClearCache` the next read asks the server again; a failed `ClearCache` keeps the cached answer. `OverrideSetup` gives `OverrideClient` its own adapter, and that adapter answers instead of the network. Removing the component cancels the request, and the promise is rejected with the code `CANCELLED`. A Java test unit runs on the JVM and has no browser transport: there a client without an adapter fails with `http-adapter`. The server half of this example is a plain JavaScript controller. A controller in TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Go, Dart, Ruby, Lua or C++ answers in the same way (see Controllers), so this section shows only the browser side in other languages.
